questions: Is a 10 mm sensor pitch with 12 mm footprints enough to keep the signal monotonic across the tape edge, or is there a dead zone when the line sits between sensors?
Does the 0.05 m lookahead cause phase lag or oscillation at the controller gains you chose? Would a shorter or longer lead be easier to control?
Is the 0.12 m wheel track and 0.03 m wheel radius able to reach roughly 1.5 m/s average on the oval and s-bend, or is the drivetrain the limiting factor?
Are any tuning constraints caused by the 0.7 kg mass or 0.14 m body length, such as slip or excessive yaw rate?

intent: Establish a compact, low-inertia baseline with five evenly spaced 12 mm sensors covering the 25 mm tape, placed 50 mm ahead of the axle. The goal is a usable platform that finishes the development tracks, so the Integrator has a stable base to tune. Next I will test whether the lookahead and sensor pitch are the right trade-off between lead time and noise.
learning: Baseline with no race data. Next iteration, use the Integrator's feedback and the first race's telemetry to test whether a wider or narrower sensor array, or a different lookahead, improves rms_error and line_loss_events.
rationale: This is iteration 0, so there is no race telemetry or integration feedback yet. The design therefore rests on the contract's physics and sensing rules, not on observed results. Five sensors at 10 mm pitch (x = -0.02, -0.01, 0, 0.01, 0.02) give a 40 mm sensing span across a 25 mm tape. With 12 mm footprints, the outer sensors still see the tape edge during moderate offsets, so the signal changes smoothly and the controller gets a graded error rather than a binary one. Sensors sit at y = 0.05 m, ahead of the axle, so the signal reads the line before the wheels reach it. That lead time should reduce oscillation at speed. Wheel track 0.12 m and wheel radius 0.03 m give a moderate turn rate per unit wheel difference and keep the base speed capable of ~1.5 m/s. Body width 0.12 m is the off-track limit at max(0.06, 0.0125 + 0.03) = 0.06 m, and widening the body cannot lift it above 0.06 m within the allowed range, so width is chosen for compactness. Body length 0.14 m and mass 0.7 kg keep yaw inertia low, which favours quick response on bends. Sensor weights are antisymmetric (-2, -1, 0, 1, 2), so the signal is zero when centred and scales with offset. The expected result is a completed run on the development tracks with moderate line-loss counts, with the main risk being oscillation from the lead sensors. I expect the Integrator to report whether the 0.05 m lookahead and 10 mm pitch are a usable base.
